articles.title: FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery
articles.abstract: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for a new use of the immunotherapy Jemperli (dostarlimab-gxly) that may allow some patients with locally advanced rectal cancer to avoid common treatments that can have a lasting impact on their daily life.

articles.title: Which Profession Has the Highest Risk of Radiation-Related Cancer Mortality?
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses findings that pilots and flight attendants have a higher risk of death from radiation-related cancers than other professions and examines what the results may mean for occupational protections for aircrew.

articles.title: ACOG Strengthens Recommendation for Fallopian Tube Removal to Prevent Ovarian Cancer
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists’ clinical practice update on opportunistic salpingectomy procedures to prevent ovarian cancer in patients with average risk.

articles.title: Months, Not Years
articles.abstract: In this narrative medicine essay, a newly graduated medical student about to start his orthopedic residency halted his training upon learning his cancer had returned and was inoperable.

articles.title: [Editorial] Microplastics and cancer: a looming threat?
articles.abstract: Microplastics are a growing global concern and have been linked to various health conditions. A study presented by Ilias Dimeas and colleagues at the 2026 European Respiratory Society conference found a higher burden of microplastics in the lungs of patients with lung cancer than in those without cancer. In the study, 70% of 100 people undergoing a bronchoscopy had detectable microplastics in at least one sample, and patients with lung cancer were more likely to have detectable microplastics in their samples than patients without lung cancer.

articles.title: [Comment] Exercise oncology: from trials and guidelines to routine clinical care
articles.abstract: In oncology practice, there are trade-offs between quality of life and survival for many therapies. Similar trade-offs exist for drug reimbursement based on therapeutic effectiveness, affected population, and cost.

articles.title: [Comment] Looking at cancer burden in Africa through a new lens
articles.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of death and disability globally, with a disproportionate rising burden in Africa.1,2 Effective policy response has been consistently hampered by fragmented and incomplete cancer surveillance data.3 For a long time, there has been an assumption that a global uniform framework for understanding cancer risk factors exists and is applicable universally.4 This concept of harmonised global data is plausible in well structured and well resourced health systems in which research and care systems are integrated—systems that exist mostly in high-income regions.

articles.title: [Comment] Personalised medicine in oncology: inequality aversion in a fast-moving field
articles.abstract: Personalised medicine has been shown to improve patient care and holds promise to further benefit treatment results. The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research provides an overview of state-of-the-art treatments and the situation in low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs). From targeted treatment using companion diagnostics, identifying targets to guide treatment decisions, to broad ‘omics testing in cancer of unknown primary and metastasised tumours, the field is vast and inequalities exist within and between countries.

articles.title: [Comment] Ethical priorities in global cancer genomics and precision oncology
articles.abstract: Amid the promise of cancer genomics and precision oncology lies complex and ethically weighty issues. Genomics and other ‘omics are undoubtedly transforming cancer care for thousands of patients annually, enabling better prognosis, access to treatments or trials, or informing relatives. Yet, these interventions overwhelmingly benefit people in high-income countries: they are failing to reach most patients with cancer who could benefit, and those who are reached could, for reasons including health system readiness or data representation and interpretation, receive no or marginal benefit to their care.

articles.title: [Comment] Inequities in access to precision oncology: shared challenges, unified blueprint
articles.abstract: Precision oncology has substantially changed the therapeutic landscape from a “one size fits all” approach to that of individualised (or personalised) treatments.1 The promise of precision oncology extends across the entire cancer continuum from prevention, early diagnosis, subtyping of tumours, treatment selection, risk-adapted therapies, development of novel anticancer medicines, and post-treatment surveillance.2 The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research focuses on the current challenges and practical solutions to faciliate wider implementation.

articles.title: [Comment] Beyond the evidence: why multistakeholder cooperation will determine whether cancer genomics reaches patients
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology presents a worrying picture.1 While the number of precision oncology drugs continues to increase,2,3 access to testing and matched therapies remains profoundly unequal, research is concentrated in high-income countries (HICs) and populations of European ancestry, and expanding testing capacity has not always translated into proportionate population-level benefit. The Commission's survey of national cancer control programmes (NCCPs), conducted in collaboration with the Union for International Cancer Control and WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) across 34 countries, found partial integration of genomics into most NCCPs, including in HICs.

articles.title: [Comment] Ecological neglect: critical oversight in precision oncology governance
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research1 examines the gap between the promise of precision oncology and its delivery across global health systems. Raffaella Casolino and colleagues argue that precision oncology has advanced with remarkable speed, yet its clinical impact and sustainability remain uneven, meaning that for much of the world, precision oncology remains just a promise. The authors argue that if the vision of precision oncology is to be realised, health systems need to generate, integrate, govern, and learn from data.

articles.title: [Comment] Affordability in the era of precision oncology
articles.abstract: Cancer drugs are increasingly unaffordable for health systems. Global spending on cancer drugs will reach US$441 billion by 2029.1 This 75% increase over 5 years cannot be explained by population ageing or changing prevalence alone. Instead, the price of cancer drugs is driving accelerated spending growth.2 Rising prices place considerable pressure on health systems, particularly when increased spending is not matched by commensurate improvements in patient health. Unfortunately, many expensive cancer drugs have highly uncertain safety and efficacy evidence at the time of market authorisation.

articles.title: [Comment] Counting who was not tested: artificial intelligence extraction of genomic and treatment data from hospital records
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable access to cancer genomics and precision oncology provides an important framework defining indicators that health systems can and should measure.1 Operationalising these indicators, however, requires substantial data infrastructure. One indicator in the Commission's Precision Oncology Access Cascade defines the group of eligible patients who receive recommended genomic testing. The number of patients tested is relatively straightforward to obtain; however, the number meeting the guideline criteria is not because this information is usually recorded as unstructured narrative text rather than as a structured field.

articles.title: [Comment] Blank spaces on the map: genomics for global cancer research
articles.abstract: For most of the history of cancer genomics, the map of our knowledge has had blank spaces on it. In the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes, for example, roughly three quarters of donors were of European descent; samples from Latin American donors made up only about 1% of the large public repositories and samples from patients of Middle Eastern descent were almost entirely absent.1

articles.title: [Comment] England's National Cancer Plan; ambition without accountability
articles.abstract: Publication of England's National Cancer Control Plan (NCCP) in February, 2026,1 marked a hard-won achievement, after years of advocacy from patients, clinicians, charities, parliamentarians, and The Lancet Oncology.2,3 The expectation was to address long-standing systemic issues in treatment delays and quality, workforce shortages, and inequalities; but hopes were quickly dashed.4 The plan had no real new money, no additional workforce capacity, no expansion of treatment infrastructure, no prioritisation, and no implementation strategy.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Re-evaluating aglatimagene in localised prostate cancer
articles.abstract: We read with great interest the Article by Theodore L DeWeese and colleagues detailing the results of the PrTK03 phase 3 trial, which evaluated the addition of aglatimagene besadenovec (CAN-2409) and valacyclovir to standard-of-care external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) for localised prostate cancer.1 We commend the investigators for executing this decade-spanning study. The biological premise—using an adenoviral vector to exert localised cytotoxicity of a systemically administered prodrug while stimulating a T-cell-mediated immune response—is scientifically sound.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Re-evaluating aglatimagene in localised prostate cancer – Authors' reply
articles.abstract: We thank Thomas Büttner and colleagues for their interest in our Article on the PrTK03 trial.1 In our trial, disease-free survival was the prospectively specified, US Food and Drug Administration-agreed primary endpoint under a Special Protocol Assessment, analysed in the intention-to-treat population and defined to include local failure, including positive biopsy, regional failure, distant metastasis, or death.1 The US Food and Drug Administration did not agree to use biochemical failure as a disease-free survival event.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Proton pump inhibitors and durvalumab in PACIFIC
articles.abstract: Leonardo Brunetti and colleagues’ post-hoc analysis of the PACIFIC trial in The Lancet Oncology addresses an important and clinically timely question: whether baseline exposure to proton pump inhibitors or antibiotics modifies the benefit of durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy in patients with unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer.1 The observed association between proton pump inhibitor exposure and inferior progression-free and overall survival in the durvalumab group, but not in the placebo group, is thought provoking.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Proton pump inhibitors and durvalumab in PACIFIC – Authors' reply
articles.abstract: We thank our colleagues for their thoughtful comments on our post-hoc analysis of PACIFIC.1 Their correspondence raises two issues: the definition of survival events and whether proton pump inhibitor exposure is causal or reflects its prescribing context.

articles.title: [News] Trump cuts childhood vaccine recommendations
articles.abstract: The US President Donald Trump has issued an executive order stressing “maximal parental choice” and cutting the number of childhood vaccines recommended by the federal government to 11 from 18.

articles.title: [News] Nigeria plans major expansion of radiotherapy capacity
articles.abstract: Africa's most populous country Nigeria plans to procure and install 35 additional linear accelerators (LINACs), substantially expanding its radiotherapy capacity. Six Cancer Centres of Excellence are also being developed, with centres in Katsina, Enugu, and Benin completed and commissioned. However, the new machines translating into wider access depends on availability of specialist staffing, maintenance, financing, and where the additional capacity is located.

articles.title: [News] Delays in cancer referrals and care lead to harm and missed diagnoses in England
articles.abstract: Late and missed diagnoses, delays in cancer care, and physical harm were partly caused by England's National Health Service (NHS) system for general practitioners (GPs) seeking specialist advice before patient referral to hospital, according to an investigation by the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB).

articles.title: [News] Increased tobacco production and cigarette imports in Africa
articles.abstract: While tobacco-leaf production across the world declined by 19% between 2012 and 2024, it increased by 9% in Africa, according to a WHO analysis published on Aug 31, 2026. Moreover, during this period, there was a more than two-times increase in cigarette imports to Africa—from US$833 million to $1·77 billion.

articles.title: [News] 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer
articles.abstract: Interim results from the phase 3 ARTEMIS-008 trial, presented by Jie Wang (Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, China), suggest risvutatug rezetecan, a B7-H3-directed antibody–drug conjugate (ADC), could be the new standard of care in relapsed small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive risvutatug rezetecan (8·0 mg/kg; n=230) or topotecan (1·2 mg/m2 on days 1–5; n=231) every 3 weeks. At a median follow-up of 12·2 months, overall survival (the primary endpoint) was significantly improved with risvutatug rezetecan compared with topotecan (18·5 vs 10·3 months; HR 0·46 [95% CI 0·35–0·62).

articles.title: [News] Kenya agrees major cuts to cancer drug prices
articles.abstract: The Kenyan Government has agreed a deal with Pfizer that could reduce the price of selected cancer medicines by seven times. Costs are expected to drop from as much as 1 million Kenyan Shillings (KSh; US$7725) to below KSh50 000 ($386) per treatment cycle for some drugs. The agreement covers nine cancers: breast, stomach, colorectal, lung, prostate, and oesophageal cancers, as well as leukaemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma.

articles.title: [News] Toxic dust around the World Trade Center
articles.abstract: On Sept 8, 2026, New York City authorities released more than 170 000 pages of documents showing that officials misled the public about toxic air quality levels after the Sept 11, 2001, attack that killed more than 2600 people at the World Trade Center (WTC). Health researchers say the documents contain little medical information that is new but confirm that carcinogens and toxins were present months after the attacks, exposing 400 000 people in lower Manhattan to smoke, dust, and combustion products.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Cancer's new anxiety: not a death sentence, but delay
articles.abstract: Throughout the history of cancer research, hyperbole has never been in short supply—whether it be Richard Nixon's war, Joe Biden's moonshot, or Cancer Research UK's 2023 declaration of a golden era. Driving such rhetoric has been the need to act against an enduring societal concern—cancer, the so-called Big C, society's number one fear.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Against cancer, not against dying: Ernest Becker in the oncology clinic
articles.abstract: When American cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker was awarded the 1974 Pulitzer Prize for his book, The Denial of Death, he had died of colorectal cancer only 2 months earlier. More than half a century later, the book feels almost uncomfortably contemporary in the oncology clinic. Although the book does not address cancer care directly, it speaks to what cancer reveals: mortality, and the symbolic structures we build to make that knowledge bearable. For Becker, identities, professions, institutions, religions, families, reputations, and achievements are ways in which the fragile self seeks continuity beyond finitude.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Sir Chris Hoy's Tour de 4 charity cycle ride returns
articles.abstract: Mention the name Chris Hoy and it's natural to picture the Olympic cyclist, who won six gold medals and one silver in Sydney, Athens, Beijing, and London between 2000 and 2012. Fans voted for him to be named as the BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2008, and he was knighted by the late Queen Elizabeth in the 2009 New Year honours list. However, over the past 2 years, Hoy has become famous for a completely different reason. In October, 2024, he revealed that he had received a terminal diagnosis of stage-4 prostate cancer, which had spread to his bones.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Differing approaches to cancer at the Edinburgh Fringe
articles.abstract: “I had cancer a couple of years ago—I don’t like to talk about it,” grinned comedian Matt Forde during his show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the world's largest arts festival, which took place in Edinburgh, UK, on Aug 7–31, 2026. With a sly grin at his audience, he added “I’m not going to use it to sell tickets for another sold out night in Edinburgh.” Forde, who is best known for his impressions of politicians, was diagnosed in July, 2023, with a chordoma, a very rare sarcoma at the base of his spine.

articles.title: [Articles] Chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab followed by maintenance pembrolizumab with or without olaparib as first-line treatment of patients with advanced BRCA non-mutated epithelial ovarian cancer (ENGOT-OV43/GOG-3036/KEYLYNK-001): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy followed by maintenance with pembrolizumab–olaparib showed a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival versus chemotherapy, suggesting that this regimen might have potential for patients with newly diagnosed BRCA non-mutated stage III–IV epithelial ovarian cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] Global burden of cancer attributable to infections in 2024: a worldwide incidence analysis
articles.abstract: Our findings highlight the importance of infection control to achieve cancer prevention. Scientifically proven, but often underused, approaches include HPV and HBV vaccination; testing and treatment of HIV, H pylori, HBV, and HCV; safe injection practices; access to condoms and pre-exposure prophylaxis to prevent HIV transmission; and screening of precancerous lesions for HPV-driven cervical and anal cancer. Our findings also inform the investment cases for research and development for new prevention tools, most notably for EBV.

articles.title: [Articles] Hypofractionated versus conventional fractionated postmastectomy radiotherapy for patients with high-risk breast cancer (CHN HYPOPMRT): 10-year outcomes from a randomised, non-inferiority, open-label, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: Hypofractionated postmastectomy radiotherapy provided durable locoregional control with no increase in severe late adverse events compared with conventional fractionation, supporting its use as a more time-efficient option than conventional fractionated radiotherapy.

articles.title: [Articles] Patient-reported symptom monitoring in patients with lung cancer (SYMPRO-Lung trial): long-term, post-hoc survival results of a multicentre, stepped-wedged, cluster-randomised clinical trial
articles.abstract: Weekly PRO symptom monitoring was associated with meaningful improvement in long-term overall survival among patients with stage I–IV lung cancer. Median overall survival was 5 months longer in the intervention group than in the control group. These findings underscore the value of implementing PRO symptom monitoring within routine care for patients with lung cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] An integrated lifestyle intervention for mitigation of adverse effects associated with androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer (STAMINA): a multicentre, randomised trial
articles.abstract: The STAMINA lifestyle intervention meets best practice guidelines, can be implemented in NHS trusts in England, and offers clinicians a clear basis for identification and prescription of a supervised exercise and dietary advice intervention to mitigate negative effects associated with ADT.

articles.title: [Articles] Development and external validation of a new prognostic model for metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma: a preregistered analysis using data from randomised clinical trials in the checkpoint inhibitor era
articles.abstract: The CPI2 model, using 14 readily available clinical parameters, demonstrated improvement in discriminative accuracy compared with the IMDC model. This classification should be further validated in other trial and observational populations and be used to reanalyse heterogeneity of treatment effects of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination regimens in trials shaping the current and future treatment landscape.

articles.title: [Articles] Long-term exposure to wildfire-related PM2·5 and overall survival of older patients with lung cancer: a retrospective, registry-based cohort study
articles.abstract: Wildfire-related PM2·5 showed greater toxicity per unit exposure than non-wildfire PM2·5. As wildfire-related PM2·5 is the fastest-growing contributor to ambient air pollution, there is an urgent need for updated strategies to manage wildfires and mitigate their effects.

articles.title: [Articles] Burden of cancer in Africa, 1990–2023: a systematic analysis from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
articles.abstract: Cancer is a growing contributor to the disease burden in Africa, with rising cases, deaths, and DALYs disproportionately affecting children, adolescents, and young adults. The increase in age-standardised mortality and DALY rates stands in sharp contrast to the ambitions of the Sustainable Development Goals for 2030 and the African Union Agenda 2063. Addressing this burden will require coordinated national and international action, with health-system strengthening and context-specific cancer-control strategies spanning prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment.

articles.title: [The Lancet Oncology Commission] Accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research: a Lancet Oncology Commission
articles.abstract: Cancer genomics and precision oncology are increasingly central to cancer care, but many health systems struggle to implement them equitably, effectively, and sustainably. This Commission defines the current global precision oncology landscape and analyses the scientific, structural, and health-system challenges shaping its delivery and impact. Findings indicate that access to cancer genomics and precision oncology remains profoundly unequal across and within countries, leaving millions of patients without guideline-indicated interventions each year.

articles.title: [Clinical Picture] Not all thoracic micronodules are metastases
articles.abstract: A 58-year-old female, lifelong non-smoker with history of Parkinson's disease, presented with a palpable right breast lump to the Odette Cancer Centre at Sunnybrook Health and Sciences Centre (Toronto, ON, Canada) in April, 2024, and was diagnosed with right-sided oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2-positive breast cancer (cT3N0). She received neoadjuvant dose dense doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab. Lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed revealing a pathological complete response.

articles.title: Chronotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors: The knowns, the unknowns, and the contested
articles.abstract: Emerging data indicate that immune checkpoint inhibitors can exhibit time-of-day-dependent effects in pre-clinical models. Furthermore, multiple retrospective clinical trials associate earlier anti-tumor treatment timing with improved outcomes. However, key questions remain regarding the reproducibility of these findings, the underlying mechanisms, and their clinical implications. This commentary discusses these open questions and provides an outlook on the field.

articles.title: Human-centric preclinical models for CAR T cell therapy in solid tumors: Where patient-derived organoids fit
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has shown promising activity in solid tumors, yet translational progress remains limited by preclinical models that incompletely capture human tumor biology. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) preserve key features of human tumors, including cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture, thereby enabling functional evaluation of CAR T cell targets, next-generation approaches, resistance mechanisms, and selected safety considerations. We discuss how PDOs complement existing preclinical platforms to support CAR T cell development for solid tumors.

articles.title: γδ T cells BiTE back at small cell lung cancer
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Ng et al. characterize and leverage cytotoxic γδ T cells in small cell lung cancer to overcome unsuccessful checkpoint blockade immunotherapy. Engaging Vδ2+ cells with a bispecific T cell engager (BiTE) bypasses the challenge of low MHC-I expression and ineffective CD8+ T cells.

articles.title: Microbial cues for a stem-like lymphoid niche
articles.abstract: While tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) broadly correlate with immunotherapy efficacy, their functional heterogeneity can translate into divergent clinical outcomes. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hu et al. uncover a microbiota-orchestrated stem-like lymphoid niche in which CD70+ ILC2s sustain progenitor exhausted T cells, and their findings redefine the functional organization underlying TLS-associated antitumor immunity.

articles.title: Teamwork makes the dream work? Ensemble learning in computational pathology
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Luo et al. report an ensemble approach that integrates five pretrained pathology foundation models into a slide-level representation to exploit their complementary information, yielding improvements in tumor subtyping, biomarker, and therapy-response prediction. This shows the potential of ensemble and multimodal approaches in computational pathology.

articles.title: Hitting KRAS G12D without the gut punch: Can immunotherapy make it last?
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Shi et al. report encouraging early-phase results combining HRS-4642, an allele-specific KRAS G12D inhibitor, with the PD-L1 inhibitor adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer. The intravenous combination was safe and well tolerated, notably sparing patients the gastrointestinal toxicity common to oral KRAS inhibitors, and achieved a promising 43% response rate at the recommended dose.

articles.title: Beyond genes and hotspots: Protein-informed interpretation of cancer mutations
articles.abstract: Interpreting the biological and clinical significance of somatic mutations in cancer genomes remains challenging. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hyeon et al. identify and map significantly mutated regions to protein domains and structural features, establishing a proteo-genomics framework for interpreting cancer mutations beyond genes and hotspots.

articles.title: The wu wei of brain metastases: When the gift of a pause is also a vulnerability
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, García-Gómez et al. show that brain-seeding cancer cells exploit an MXD4-dependent proliferative pause that enables survival under stress before metastatic outgrowth. By restraining MYC and activating protective stress responses, this pause becomes an Achilles’ heel, potentially targetable to eradicate micrometastases before clinical relapse.

articles.title: Tumor cells recruit macrophage bodyguards to outlast chemotherapy
articles.abstract: In Cell Press Blue, Carvalho et al. identify spatially organized tumor-macrophage niches, EMT-like CD44high cancer cells paired with SPP1/PARP14high macrophages, that drive chemoresistance in bladder cancer. PARP14 inhibition can flip this protective niche into an inflammatory, cisplatin-sensitizing state.

articles.title: Beyond BMI: The diet-microbiome context of the obesity paradox
articles.abstract: In Nature, Desharnais et al. show that in diverse mouse models, anti-PD-1 sensitivity is more closely linked to diet-microbiome-metabolite ecosystem than to obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction. Their findings reinforce body mass index (BMI) as an incomplete proxy for host biology and suggest strategies to improve anti-PD-1 efficacy without inducing obesity.

articles.title: γδ T cells modulate anti-tumor immunity in small cell lung cancer
articles.abstract: Ng et al. show that γδ T cells infiltrate SCLC and have cancer-fighting abilities. These cells can be harnessed through multiple therapeutics to kill SCLC, including through MHC-independent recognition mechanisms via BTN2A1. Notably, γδ T cell infiltration is clinically relevant in SCLC, with high levels predictive of improved outcomes with αPD-L1.

articles.title: Ensemble learning of pathology foundation models for precision oncology
articles.abstract: Luo et al. develop ELF, a framework that ensembles five pathology foundation models to generate unified representations from whole-slide images. Trained on nearly 54,000 slides across 20 anatomical sites, ELF outperforms individual foundation models in disease classification, biomarker detection, and prediction of response to chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy.

articles.title: UniCure: A multi-modal model for predicting personalized cancer therapy response
articles.abstract: Chen et al. present UniCure, a multi-modal foundation model that predicts drug-induced transcriptomic responses across diverse cellular contexts. By bridging cancer cell line data with patient-derived models, UniCure enables personalized drug prioritization and patient stratification, with its predicted therapeutic rankings correlating strongly with clinical survival outcomes in real-world cohorts.

articles.title: Myeloid reprogramming generates myeloid-derived activating cells to potentiate radiotherapy and suppress metastasis
articles.abstract: Ji et al. show that radiotherapy induces a TET2-dependent epitranscriptomic program in myeloid cells that promotes immunosuppressive M-MDSC differentiation. TET2 loss preserves caRNA m5C-MBD6 signaling, restores IRF3-IFN-I activation, generates myeloid-derived activating cells, and enhances radiotherapy-induced antitumor immunity.

articles.title: Intratumoral Bacillus cereus orchestrates stem-like lymphoid niches to potentiate immunotherapy response in hepatocellular carcinoma
articles.abstract: Hu et al. integrate spatial multi-omics to identify stem-like lymphoid niches (SLNs) organized by CD70+ ILC2s and Tpex cells that predict PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy responses in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). They reveal that Bacillus cereus-PI-PLC increases SLN abundance and synergizes with PD-L1 blockade, highlighting microbiota-driven enhancement of cancer immunotherapy through SLNs therapeutically in HCC.

articles.title: Proteo-genomics-guided interpretation of somatic mutations in cancer genomes
articles.abstract: Hyeon et al. integrate protein structures with population-scale cancer genomics data to characterize significantly mutated regions in 173 cancer-relevant genes. These regions align with functional domains, three-dimensional structural constraints, and gene-specific biology, providing a framework for classifying mutation patterns in cancer genes and prioritizing sparsely annotated variants for clinical interpretation.

articles.title: A transient MXD4-dependent proliferative pause enables survival of brain micrometastases
articles.abstract: García-Gómez et al. identify a transient state, termed the proliferative pause, that enables the survival of micrometastases during vascular co-option by buffering organ-imposed stress. Targeting vulnerabilities associated with this state suppresses metastatic progression and relapse, revealing opportunities for preventive intervention.

articles.title: Chemotherapy enhances cancer vaccine efficacy and expands stem-like TCF1+CD8+ T cells
articles.abstract: Noblecourt et al. show that chemotherapy acts as an immunological adjuvant by expanding TCF1+CD8+ T cells during vaccine priming, thereby enhancing vaccine-induced anti-tumor immunity. These findings provide a rationale for combining chemotherapy, cancer vaccines, and PD-1 blockade in the clinic.

articles.title: Chemotherapy-free phase 1/2 trial of HRS-4642 plus adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic cancer
articles.abstract: Shi et al. report the first clinical study of the selective KRAS G12D inhibitor HRS-4642 combined with the anti-PD-L1 antibody adebrelimab in heavily pretreated patients with KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic cancer. The chemotherapy-free regimen demonstrates a manageable safety profile and preliminary antitumor activity, supporting its feasibility as a targeted strategy in this molecularly defined subset.

articles.title: Retraction Notice to: Taxanes trigger cancer cell killing in vivo by inducing non-canonical T cell cytotoxicity
Concurrent administration of BCMA and GPRC5D CAR T cells for advanced multiple myeloma.
articles.abstract: B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)- and G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D)-directed therapies have shown high efficacy in the treatment of relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, with multiple new immune therapies now approved. Preclinical studies have shown that the expression of BCMA and GPRC5D is heterogeneous in malignant plasma cells. We conducted a phase 1 dose-escalation trial of the BCMA chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy MCARH125 alone or in combination with the GPRC5D CAR T-cell therapy MCARH109 in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Patients were treated across 3 dose levels, with the primary objective of establishing the safety of concurrent infusion. We treated 15 patients across 3 dose levels, including 6 patients who received MCARH125 alone and 9 patients treated with the concurrent infusion of MCARH125 and MCARH109. One patient each with MCARH 125 alone and the coinfusion of MCARH125 and MCARH109 developed immune effector cell-associated hemophagocytic syndrome. There were no instances of grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome or immune effector cell-associated neurologic syndrome. The overall response for coinfusion was 78%, with a median progression-free survival of 18.2 months. Correlative analysis suggests that antigen loss may be an important mechanism of resistance even with dual-antigen targeting, and we show, to our knowledge for the first time that expansion of 1 CAR population may limit expansion of the second population because patients treated with dual CARs had significantly less BCMA CAR expansion compared with patients treated with BCMA CAR alone, despite equivalent BCMA CAR T-cell doses at infusion. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT05431608.

articles.title: Prognostic associations between patient-reported outcomes and progression-free and overall survival in advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma with PD-L1 TAP score ≥ 5%: results from the RATIONALE-305 trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: In RATIONALE-305, tislelizumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival (OS) versus placebo plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (GC/GEJC) with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor area positivity (TAP) score ≥ 5% and in all patients. Here, we present a three-component joint model (JM) developed to evaluate associations between patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and risk of progression-free survival (PFS) and OS events. METHODS: Longitudinal PRO data were analyzed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-STO22. The JM linked: (1) a linear mixed model (LMM) for change from baseline in PRO scores; (2) a Cox model for time to recurrent symptomatic deterioration (RS-D); and (3) a Cox model to evaluate the RS-D event frailty prediction of PFS and OS. RESULTS: 475 patients in the PD-L1 ≥ 5% subgroup (tislelizumab + chemotherapy, n = 238; placebo + chemotherapy, n = 237) were evaluated. In PFS and OS LMMs, tislelizumab + chemotherapy versus placebo + chemotherapy was associated with improved GHS/QoL (global health status/quality of life) (p = 0.01) and reduced dietary restrictions (p = 0.05). In the OS LMM, tislelizumab + chemotherapy was associated with reduced upper GI symptoms (p = 0.01) and reductions in dietary restrictions (p = 0.02). RS-D in GHS/QoL, pain, and dietary restrictions were leading predictors of PFS risk. Across all QLQ-C30 and QLQ-STO22 domains, tislelizumab plus chemotherapy significantly reduced the risk of progression or death (PFS HRs 0.55-0.65; 35-45% reduction) and death (OS HRs 0.65-0.73; 27-35% reduction); all p ≤ 0.01. CONCLUSION: PROs have significant prognostic value for disease progression and survival in patients with PD-L1 TAP score ≥ 5%. REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT03777657 ( http://clinicaltrials.gov ). Stomach and gastroesophageal junction cancers are among the most common and deadly cancers worldwide, and patients often suffer significant symptoms that reduce their quality of life. While patient-reported outcomes (i.e., surveys where patients describe their own symptoms and wellbeing) are known to matter in cancer care, it has been unclear how changes in these reports over time relate to disease progression and survival. This study linked patients’ ongoing symptom reports with their clinical outcomes in a large clinical trial of the immunotherapy tislelizumab combined with chemotherapy. The results demonstrated that worsening health-related quality of life, pain, and dietary difficulties were early warning signs of disease progression or death, while treatment with tislelizumab consistently protected against both. These findings support using patient-reported disease-specific symptoms as meaningful clinical tools to guide treatment decisions and improve care for patients with advanced gastric cancer.

articles.title: Combination of oral fluoropyrimidines and EGFR-directed antibodies in frail patients with metastatic colorectal cancer: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence of treatment strategies in frail patients (i.e. not fit for combination therapies) with unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is limited to dose-reduced doublet regimens or oral fluoropyrimidines (FP) with bevacizumab. We conducted a systematic review analyzing evidence for oral FPs with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-directed monoclonal antibodies for patients with RAS wild-type (WT) mCRC across treatment lines. METHODS: We searched PubMed and Cochrane Library for phase II and phase III studies evaluating oral FPs (capecitabine, S-1 or trifluridine/tipiracil (FTD/TPI)) plus EGFR-directed monoclonal antibody (panitumumab or cetuximab) in mCRC. Outcomes included efficacy and safety. RESULTS: Seven publications met inclusion criteria (n = 262 patients). First-line data was limited to elderly cohorts receiving capecitabine plus cetuximab or panitumumab with a median progression-free survival (PFS)/median overall survival (OS) of 7.2/17.1 months (cetuximab) and 7.5/23.7 months (panitumumab), respectively. In third-line and beyond, median PFS for the combination of FTD/TPI plus cetuximab or panitumumab ranged from 2.4 (cetuximab) to 5.8 months (panitumumab), and OS from 9.8 (cetuximab) to 14.2 months (panitumumab). S-1 plus cetuximab was associated with a median PFS of 5.5 months and OS of 13.6 months. CONCLUSION: While capecitabine should not be used together with anti-EGFR antibodies, FTD/TPI in combination with an EGFR-directed antibody appears feasible, shows promising activity and manageable toxicity profile in RAS WT mCRC potentially offering an alternative for frail patients; prospective trials are needed.

articles.title: Protective effect of N-acetylcysteine on oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy in colorectal cancer: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy (OIPN) is a dose-limiting adverse effect of FOLFOX chemotherapy in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. We aimed to evaluate the protective effect of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) against OIPN. Additionally, we investigated its mechanistic effects on serum biomarkers including total antioxidant capacity (TAC), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and neurotensin. METHODS: Forty-six patients with stage III or high-risk stage II CRC receiving adjuvant modified FOLFOX-6 chemotherapy were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either oral NAC 1200 mg (effervescent tablets or granules) or placebo one hour before each oxaliplatin infusion for four cycles. Serum levels of TAC, IL-6, and neurotensin were measured before and after treatment. Neuropathy was assessed using the FACT/GOG-NTX-12 and NCI-CTCAE scales, and pain was estimated by using the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form. RESULTS: Neurotensin was significantly decreased in the NAC group compared to controls after treatment (P < 0.001), and was significantly lower post-treatment versus pre-treatment in the NAC group (P = 0.001). IL-6 was significantly reduced in the NAC group versus controls after treatment (P < 0.001), and significantly decreased post-treatment in both groups (P < 0.05). FACT/GOG-NTX-12 and NCI-CTCAE scores were significantly lower in the NAC group at the end of the first two cycles and at the end of treatment (P < 0.05). Pain interference, but not pain severity, was significantly reduced in the NAC group at both time points (P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: NAC administration during FOLFOX chemotherapy significantly reduced OIPN severity, pain interference, and serum levels of IL-6 and neurotensin, suggesting both clinical and mechanistic neuroprotective effects. CLINICAL REGISTRATION: The study was is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT07391163).

articles.title: Comparable efficacy of extraoral and intraoral photobiomodulation in preventing oral mucositis during high-dose methotrexate therapy in pediatric oncology: A single-blind randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This prospective randomized controlled clinical study compared intraoral (IO) and extraoral (EO) photobiomodulation (PBM) for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced oral mucositis (OM) in pediatric oncology patients. METHODS: A total of 155 patients (1-18 years), receiving high-dose methotrexate (HDMTX) for leukemia, lymphoma, or osteosarcoma, were randomized to PBM-IO (n = 73) or PBM-EO (n = 82). Preventive PBM was administered daily from hospital admission through discharge. Both protocols used red light with equivalent dosimetry (660 nm, 100 mW, 1 J per point). PBM-EO required 30 s/session, whereas PBM-IO required approximately 6 min, excluding patient handling time. OM occurrence, severity (WHO scale), plaque index, and pain (numeric rating scale) were assessed on days 0, 3, 5, and 10 after HDMTX infusion. RESULTS: The overall OM occurrence was 35.5%, with no significant difference between PBM-IO (41.1%) and PBM-EO (30.5%) groups (p = 0.168). No statistically significant differences were observed between groups for OM severity, pain, salivary pH, or plaque index at any time point (p > 0.05). Multivariable ordinal logistic regression demonstrated that PBM modality was not independently associated with OM severity. As expected, increasing age (OR = 1.14; 95% CI: 1.04-1.25; p = 0.004) and higher HDMTX dose (OR = 1.24; 95% CI: 1.03-1.49; p = 0.021) were significantly associated with greater OM severity. Median pain scores remained 0 at all assessment points in both groups. CONCLUSION: Extraoral PBM demonstrated comparable effectiveness to intraoral for OM prevention in pediatric patients undergoing HDMTX chemotherapy, while reducing application time.

articles.title: Bolus-only versus bolus plus continuous infusion hydromorphone for refractory cancer pain: a prospective, multicenter, randomized noninferiority trial.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Refractory cancer pain (RCP) remains difficult to manage despite guideline-based therapy. Patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) is increasingly used, yet the optimal administration mode remains unclear. METHODS: In this prospective, multicenter, randomized, non-inferiority trial, patients with refractory cancer pain were enrolled between December 1, 2018, and August 31, 2022, and randomly assigned to either a bolus-only PCIA group (Group B) or a bolus plus continuous infusion group (Group BC). Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS). The primary endpoint was the pain relief rate at 72 h after PCIA initiation, defined as the proportion of patients achieving a ≥ 50% reduction in resting pain intensity from baseline. Non-inferiority was evaluated using the 90% confidence interval (CI) for the between-group difference, with a predefined non-inferiority margin of - 10%. RESULTS: A total of 226 patients were randomized. with 104 assigned to Group B and 111 to Group BC. Both groups showed significant reductions in resting NRS scores and breakthrough cancer pain (BTcP) NRS scores from T1 to T6 compared with baseline (all P < 0.05). At 72 h, the pain relief rate was 89.4% in Group B and 94.2% in Group BC. The between-group difference yielded a 90% CI of - 11.2% to 1.1%, which crossed the predefined non-inferiority margin. Therefore, non-inferiority of Group B compared with Group BC was not demonstrated. The incidence of PCIA-related adverse events was comparable between the two groups. CONCLUSION: Non-inferiority of bolus-only PCIA compared with bolus plus continuous infusion was not established. Nevertheless, both PCIA administration modes provided effective analgesia and demonstrated favorable safety profiles in patients with refractory cancer pain. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR1800020014. Registered 19 November 2018, https://www.chictr.org.cn/showprojEN.html?proj=32731.

articles.title: Impact of remote management using patient-reported outcomes on pain and anxiety after breast biopsy: the BIO-PSY randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Although breast biopsy is a routine procedure, it often triggers significant pain and anxiety. Pre-procedural distress has been associated with increased pain and discomfort, and persistent post-biopsy distress may affect psychological and treatment-related outcomes. However, post-biopsy care still lacks standardized follow-up. This study evaluated whether remote monitoring using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) triggering targeted interventions could improve pain and anxiety management after breast biopsy. METHODS: BIO-PSY was a French, monocentric, open-labelled, randomized controlled trial. Patients aged ≥ 18 years undergoing breast biopsy were randomized (1:1:1) to daily phone-based PROs (phone contact with a psycho-oncologist for 3 days), e-PROs (electronic interface for 3 days), or standard care. Alerts generated based on PROs thresholds prompted tailored interventions. The primary endpoint was pain on day 4 (0-10 numerical rating scale, phone-assessed). Secondary outcomes included pain at day 10; anxiety and perceived aesthetic impact (days 4 and 10); insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index) at day 10; and strategies for symptoms management. RESULTS: Among 193 patients, pain was negligible (median = 0), stable, and not statistically different between arms at day 4 and 10 (p > 0.05). The proportion of patients with clinically significant anxiety was lower in the experimental arms than in the control arm at day 4 (p < 0.001) and was lower at day 10 only in the phone-based PRO arm (adjusted p = 0.008). CONCLUSION: Pain after breast biopsy was well controlled across all arms. Remote monitoring using PROs may reduce anxiety, especially with human intervention, supporting its integration into routine post-biopsy care. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT04456920 (registered on June 23, 2020).

articles.title: Tambotatug Pelitecan in Small-Cell Lung Cancer after Platinum-Based Therapy.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tambotatug pelitecan (known as Tam-Peli, a new antibody-drug conjugate that targets the immune-checkpoint molecule B7-H3) showed promising clinical efficacy in patients with relapsed extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer in early-phase trials. METHODS: In this phase 3, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial, we assigned eligible patients with small-cell lung cancer that had progressed after first-line platinum-based therapy in a 1:1 ratio to receive tambotatug pelitecan or topotecan. The primary end point was overall survival. The key secondary end points were progression-free survival and objective response as assessed by investigators. Here, we report the results from the prespecified interim analysis. RESULTS: A total of 451 patients underwent randomization: 225 were assigned to receive tambotatug pelitecan and 226 to receive topotecan. Overall survival was significantly longer with tambotatug pelitecan than with topotecan - a median of 13.3 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.1 to could not be estimated), as compared with 9.4 months (95% CI, 7.7 to 10.5); the stratified hazard ratio for death was 0.46 (95% CI, 0.35 to 0.62; P<0.001). Treatment with tambotatug pelitecan also resulted in significantly longer progression-free survival than treatment with topotecan (median, 7.4 months [95% CI, 6.1 to 7.6] vs. 2.8 months [95% CI, 1.8 to 3.0]; stratified hazard ratio, 0.29 [95% CI, 0.23 to 0.37]; P<0.001). A confirmed objective response occurred in 59.1% of the patients in the tambotatug pelitecan group, as compared with 9.7% of those in the topotecan group (P<0.001). The overall incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher was lower with tambotatug pelitecan than with topotecan (55.4% vs. 77.9%). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with relapsed small-cell lung cancer after platinum-based therapy, treatment with tambotatug pelitecan resulted in longer overall survival, longer progression-free survival, and a higher percentage of patients with an objective response than treatment with topotecan, with a lower incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher. (Funded by the Innovative Drug Research and Development National Science and Technology Major Project and MediLink Therapeutics; TAISHAN-302 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06612151.).

articles.title: Artificial capnothorax versus single-lung ventilation in minimally invasive esophagectomy for esophageal cancer: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial capnothorax during surgery potentially increases the risk of tumor cell dissemination and impacts survival. This trial aimed to investigate the effect of artificial capnothorax on the prognosis of patients with esophageal cancer who underwent minimally invasive esophagectomy. METHODS: This prospective, randomized controlled trial was conducted in two high-volume hospitals in China. Between August 2019 and January 2020, 110 patients with resectable esophageal cancer were randomized to undergo single-lung ventilation ( n = 55) or capnothorax procedures ( n = 55). The analysis was based on the intention-to-treat principle. The final follow-up occurred in January 2023. RESULTS: A total of 110 patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. After surgery, the incidence of patients exhibiting incremental changes in circulating tumor cell levels was 18.6% (8/43) in the capnothorax group and 2.7% (1/37) in the single-lung ventilation group ( P = 0.033) (mean changes, -3.9 ± 3.4 [FU/3 mL] vs. -2.4 ± 2.9 [FU/3 mL], respectively; P = 0.039). Compared with the capnothorax group, the single-lung ventilation group had better 3-year overall survival rates (81.6%, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 72.4-92.0% vs. 65.2%, 95% CI: 59.3-78.8%; P = 0.049) and disease-free survival rates (81.6%, 95% CI: 72.4-93.0% vs. 61.6%, 95% CI: 50.1-75.7%; P = 0.019). Multivariate analysis indicated that artificial pneumothorax potentially impaired overall survival (hazard ratio [HR]: 2.35, 95% CI: 1.05-5.24; P = 0.037) and disease-free survival (HR: 2.70, 95% CI: 1.23-5.94; P = 0.014). CONCLUSIONS: Artificial capnothorax appears to be associated with poor oncological outcomes in patients with esophageal cancer. Single-lung ventilation in minimally invasive esophagectomy is safer and more favorable than capnothorax. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ( http://chictr.org.cn ), ChiCTR1900025262.

articles.title: Antibody-Drug Conjugates in Biliary Tract Cancer: Current Evidence, Emerging Targets, and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Biliary tract cancer (BTC) is a heterogeneous group of malignancies with limited systemic treatment options and poor prognosis. While immunochemotherapy has become the first-line standard, second-line therapy remains inadequate. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality leveraging antigen-specific targeting to deliver potent cytotoxic payloads. This review provides a comprehensive, multi-target appraisal of the ADC landscape in BTC. RECENT FINDINGS: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), supported by DESTINY-PanTumor02 (ORR 22%) and HERB (ORR 36.4%) trials, received 2024 FDA tumor-agnostic approval for HER2-positive solid tumors including BTC. Zanidatamab achieved 41.3% ORR in HERIZON-BTC-01, securing BTC-specific regulatory approval. BL-B01D1, an EGFR×HER3 bispecific ADC, demonstrated preliminary BTC activity (ORR 28.6%) without reported interstitial lung disease in the BTC cohort, though sample size and follow-up remain limited, while its phase III nasopharyngeal carcinoma trial established proof of concept for bispecific ADCs. BL-M05D1 phase I results (ASCO 2026) provided the first clinical evidence for Claudin18.2 ADCs in BTC (ORR 42.5%). Trop2-directed ADCs show theoretical applicability across solid tumors given 69.5% high-expression prevalence, but BTC-specific clinical data are absent. B7-H3 and CD44v5 represent emerging targets with early clinical or preclinical validation. This review provides a unified framework for navigating the rapidly evolving multi-target ADC landscape in BTC. Critical challenges remain, including the absence of phase III randomized trials, tumor heterogeneity, optimal biomarker-guided patient selection, and rational combination strategies with immunotherapy. Standardization of HER2 testing and broader molecular profiling will be essential to realize the clinical potential of ADCs in this historically treatment-refractory disease. Biliary obstruction and hepatic impairment, common in BTC, require ADC-specific pharmacokinetic vigilance and graded toxicity monitoring.

articles.title: Later-line Treatment Selection in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: Trifluridine/Tipiracil Plus Bevacizumab, Regorafenib, and Fruquintinib.
articles.abstract: Later-line therapy for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) increasingly requires selection among treatments with different mechanisms, toxicity profiles, and sequencing evidence. Trifluridine/tipiracil plus bevacizumab has robust randomized evidence from SUNLIGHT, but objective response remains uncommon and hematologic toxicity can limit treatment delivery in heavily pretreated patients. Regorafenib and fruquintinib are minimally myelosuppressive oral alternatives, yet they differ in dose strategy, hepatotoxicity, hand-foot skin reaction, hypertension, and proteinuria. This narrative review updates pivotal and recent evidence and proposes an evidence-informed framework that treats hematologic reserve as a clinical fitness construct rather than a fixed laboratory threshold. We additionally examine the clinical implications of low response rates, prior anti-angiogenic exposure, emerging molecular predictors including KRAS G12, evidence in older or vulnerable patients, and recent phase III developments. Current data do not support a validated molecular biomarker for choosing among these three options, and no randomized head-to-head comparison of regorafenib and fruquintinib exists. Accordingly, treatment selection should be individualized according to prior therapies, toxicity vulnerability, organ function, tumor tempo, and patient goals. Hypertension and proteinuria are important selection factors but may also be modifiable treatment-delivery factors. The proposed algorithms and adverse-event radar chart are intended as practical visual syntheses rather than validated guidelines or formal cross-trial comparisons.

articles.title: Feasibility and safety of an exercise-based prehabilitation intervention before cancer surgery: a pilot randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The study aimed to assess the feasibility and safety of an exercise-based prehabilitation intervention and explore preliminary clinical outcomes in breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer patients awaiting surgery in a large regional healthcare service. METHODS: Patients with breast, prostate, or colorectal cancer scheduled for surgery were recruited at a single study centre and randomised (1:1) to prehabilitation or usual care. The intervention involved supervised aerobic exercise training 2-3 days per week before surgery. Usual care involved standard cancer treatment. Feasibility was assessed through recruitment, attendance, adherence, and attrition rates. Safety was evaluated via adverse event monitoring. Exploratory analyses evaluated group-by-time changes in cardiorespiratory fitness, health-related quality of life, and fatigue from baseline to the pre-surgery and post-surgery assessment timepoints, with 30-day post-operative outcomes (complications and length of stay) also collected. RESULTS: Of 47 potentially eligible patients approached and screened, 23 were recruited and randomised, and completed baseline assessments. Twenty participants (prehabilitation n = 11, usual care n = 9) completed the pre- and T1 and T2 assessments. Participants attended an average of 5.25 ± 2.16 prehabilitation sessions. Attendance, adherence, completeness, and attrition rates were 91.3%, 82.6%, 85.7%, and 13%, respectively. Five adverse events were recorded in the prehabilitation group (fatigue, n = 3; muscular pain in the extremities, n = 2); all were grade 1. No significant group-by-time interactions were observed for cardiorespiratory fitness, health-related quality of life, or fatigue. CONCLUSIONS: Among participants who commenced prehabilitation, attendance, adherence, and completeness were 91.3%, 82.6%, and 85.7%, respectively. No serious adverse events were observed. Exploratory clinical outcome estimates were imprecise and did not support firm conclusions regarding intervention effectiveness. Recruitment limitations and the small heterogeneous sample also preclude broader conclusions regarding feasibility.

articles.title: A cluster-randomized trial of the school-based 'Superprotegidas' behavioral intervention to improve HPV vaccination uptake in Colombian girls.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study evaluated the effect of Superprotegidas, a behavioral intervention designed to increase HPV vaccination rates among girls and their caregivers in a Colombian municipality, following the Phase III framework of the ORBIT Model for Behavioral Treatment Development. METHODS: A two-arm randomized clinical trial was conducted with schools as the unit of randomization. The intervention, based on the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior model (COMB), included a pedagogical workshop for girls, a letter, an open chat, multimedia messages, and parental reminders. RESULTS: A total of 77 girl-caregiver pairs (154 participants; girls aged 9-14) were enrolled: 42 pairs in the intervention group and 35 in the control group. Post-intervention vaccination rates were significantly higher in the intervention group (52.4%) compared to the control group (28.6%) (OR, 2.75 [95% CI: 1.06-7.12]). Predictors of vaccination, in addition to intervention participation, included lower girl's school level and higher scores on several behavioral drivers of the COM-B model (awareness of vaccine efficacy against cancer, awareness of vaccine safety, vaccine availability in schools, reflective motivation for cancer prevention, and automatic motivation related to vaccine advantages) as well as higher caregiver's self-efficacy. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that the Superprotegidas program increased HPV vaccination rates among age-eligible girls. As the program was implemented with existing program resources, and the findings also suggest that the program could be implemented in similar school-based settings.

articles.title: Extracorporeal photopheresis for the treatment of steroid-refractory immune related adverse events from immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy: a multi-center phase Ib/II clinical trial.
articles.abstract: Severe immune-related adverse events (irAE) in cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) require treatment interruption and immunosuppression. Based on prior preclinical data, in this prospective, single arm, non-randomized phase-Ib/II clinical trial we test the activity of Extracorporeal Photopheresis (ECP) against steroid-refractory irAEs in 30 patients (EudraCT-No.:2021-002073-26). The primary endpoint is the evaluation of the safety of ECP treatment for patients with ICI-induced irAEs. The study meets its pre-specified primary endpoint of less than 50% of patients developing ECP-related severe adverse events (SAE). No ECP-related SAE is observed and ECP-related AEs are reported in 20% (6/30) of patients. Overall response rate for all irAEs is 96.3% (CI 81.0-99.91). Colitis-, hepatitis- and dermatitis-specific response rates are 100% (13/13), 86.7% (13/15) and 100% (3/3), respectively. Secondary endpoints include the assessment of response rate of irAE and overall survival. ECP therapy is associated with reduced granzyme-A/B/K, T-bet, interferon-γ and TNF in peripheral T cells and pro-inflammatory gene-expression in the intestinal tract. The 12-month overall survival rate is 84.3% (CI 63.4%-93.8%). Response correlates with a decrease in inflammatory gene expression in the intestinal tract. These results suggest that ECP is a safe treatment option for SR-irAEs and warrant further investigation in subsequent randomized clinical trials.

articles.title: Avatar-led digital health intervention for sexual and gender minority young adult smoking cessation: randomized controlled pilot trial.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Accessible, culturally-tailored interventions are needed to address the high prevalence of cigarette smoking and the challenges to cessation experienced by sexual and gender minority (SGM) young adults. This study evaluated, in a randomized, controlled pilot trial, the acceptability, preliminary cessation-related outcomes, and impact on theory-based change processes of the SGM-tailored, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy-based Empowered, Queer, Quitting, and Living (EQQUAL) digital program relative to the National Cancer Institute's Smokefree.gov program. METHODS: Participants were SGM young adults, aged 18-30, who smoked at least weekly. Participants were randomized 1:1 to either EQQUAL or Smokefree.gov, both of which included a web app and text messaging. Outcomes were assessed at 3 months post-randomization, and smoking abstinence was biochemically-verified. RESULTS: The sample included 124 participants (n = 63 in EQQUAL, n = 61 in Smokefree.gov). On the primary acceptability outcomes, overall satisfaction was descriptively higher in the EQQUAL arm (68.8% vs. 60.0%; odds ratio [OR] = 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.50 to 2.78), and EQQUAL usability ratings exceeded the acceptable benchmark score of 68. The average number of EQQUAL digital sessions completed was 1.4 (of 6). On the primary cessation outcomes, biochemically-verified 7-day point prevalence abstinence was higher in EQQUAL than Smokefree.gov (11.1% vs. 4.9%; OR = 1.89, 95% CI = 0.45 to 9.66). Change in readiness to quit and cigarettes per day were similar between arms, as were outcomes of theory-based change processes. CONCLUSIONS: EQQUAL demonstrated potential benefits over Smokefree.gov on acceptability and cessation, albeit with a lack of robust effect on theory-based change processes. Increased engagement with the web-based portion of the program may be needed to improve outcomes. IMPLICATIONS: Accessible and effective smoking cessation interventions for sexual and gender minority young adults are needed to address the high prevalence of smoking in this population. This pilot randomized controlled trial demonstrated promising acceptability and cessation outcomes of the Empowered, Queer, Quitting, and Living program, a digital smoking cessation intervention tailored for sexual and gender minority young adults. A larger trial of the intervention is now warranted. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT05847673.

articles.title: Entinostat plus exemestane for hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer: long-term overall survival results from the EOC103A3101 randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: The addition of entinostat, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, to exemestane has demonstrated improved progression-free survival (PFS) in hormone receptor-positive (HR + ), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) advanced breast cancer (ABC) following endocrine therapy failure in the EOC103A3101 randomized trial (NCT03538171). This study reports long-term overall survival (OS) results. In this study, 354 patients with HR + /HER2- ABC that had recurred or progressed after endocrine therapy were randomized (2:1) to receive entinostat plus exemestane (n = 235) or placebo plus exemestane (n = 119). After a median follow-up of 31.8 months, the median OS was 38.6 months (95% confidence interval [CI]: 29.6-44.0) in the entinostat-exemestane group versus 29.2 months (95% CI: 22.5-41.6) in the placebo-exemestane group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.83, 95% CI: 0.62-1.10, P = 0.184). The entinostat-exemestane group demonstrated more pronounced OS benefits when adjusting subsequent antitumor therapies such as cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors, or the combination of endocrine therapy, CDK4/6 inhibitors, and chemotherapy. The sensitivity analysis based on the per-protocol set showed more significant OS benefits. The median time to post-discontinuation chemotherapy and chemotherapy-free survival in the entinostat-exemestane group were 11.7 and 9.3 months, respectively, compared to 6.8 and 5.6 months in the placebo-exemestane group (both P < 0.05). Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 65.5% of patients in the entinostat-exemestane group, without new safety signals observed. In conclusion, among patients with HR + /HER2- ABC after endocrine therapy failure, entinostat plus exemestane was associated with a numerically longer OS, with an acceptable safety profile.

articles.title: Anbalcabtagene autoleucel (PD-1 and TIGIT knockdown CD19 CAR T-cell therapy) for relapsed or refractory LBCL: the CRC01-01 trial.
articles.abstract: Anbalcabtagene autoleucel (anbal-cel) is a CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy incorporating dual PD-1 and TIGIT knockdown to enhance antitumor function and durability. We report results from a phase 1 and 2 study in patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. In phase 2, 79 patients received anbal-cel, and its efficacy was evaluated in 73 patients. The complete response (CR) and partial response rates were 67.1% and 8.2%, respectively. Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 6.04 months (95% confidence interval, 4.34-16.46), and the 6-, 12-, and 18-month PFS rates were 50.9%, 41.1%, and 35.2%, respectively. Median overall survival (OS) was not reached, with 12- and 18-month OS rates of 66.6% and 57.3%, respectively. CAR T-cell expansion (Cmax) was significantly greater in responders than in nonresponders (median Cmax, 20 403 vs 8580 copies per μg). Patients were categorized into long-term response (LR) group or non-LR group based on sustained CR at 6 months. Reduced PD-1 and TIGIT expression on CAR+ T cells was observed in the LR group. Most patients (97.5%) experienced grade ≥3 adverse events, most commonly neutropenia (93.7%), followed by thrombocytopenia (41.8%) and anemia (30.4%). Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurological events occurred in 57.0% and 13.9% of patients, respectively. Grade 3 CRS occurred in 8.9% of patients, with no grade 4 events reported, and grade ≥3 neurological events occurred in 3.8% of patients. Serious infections occurred in 25.3% of patients, including grade 5 infection reported in 3 patients. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as #NCT04836507.

articles.title: [Policy Review] Balancing benefits, costs, and harms: policy implications of expanding cancer susceptibility testing from genetics clinics to the general population
articles.abstract: Cancer susceptibility testing is rapidly advancing beyond specialist genetics clinics into routine oncology and population-level genomics initiatives. This expansion positions germline pathogenic variants in cancer susceptibility genes and polygenic risk scores as crucial tools for precision prevention, surveillance, and early detection. However, implementation has outpaced the evidence needed to justify testing at scale, particularly in well populations. For a small number of first-wave genes—including BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1, and MSH2—cancer risks are well established and downstream medical interventions are supported by substantial observational evidence, albeit with an absence of randomised trials.

articles.title: [Review] Cancer and the microbiome: from association to intervention
articles.abstract: The gut microbiome is increasingly recognised as a clinically modifiable determinant of efficacy and toxicity across systemic cancer therapies, with the most mature evidence in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). The composition and function of intestinal microbes can influence treatment outcomes by affecting immune priming, antigen presentation, host–microbial co-metabolism, drug biotransformation, and epithelial barrier integrity. In melanoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, and renal cell carcinoma, higher microbial diversity, ecological stability, and enrichment of immunostimulatory pathways have been associated with improved ICI response and survival.

articles.title: Toward the next generation of CAR T cell therapies for cancer
articles.abstract: CAR T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of blood cancers but faces persistent challenges in solid tumors. In this review, Usta and Mackall synthesize clinical lessons, next-generation engineering strategies, and emerging in vivo manufacturing approaches to define opportunities for broader, safer, and more effective CAR T cell therapies.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of ifupinostat in relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a multicenter, single-arm phase 2 study.
articles.abstract: Ifupinostat (BEBT-908) is a novel dual-targeted inhibitor of histone deacetylase (HDACs) and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase alpha (PI3Kα). We evaluated the efficacy and safety of ifupinostat monotherapy in patients with relapsed or refractory (r/r) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) after at least 2 prior lines of systemic therapy. Eligible participants received intravenous ifupinostat at 22.5 mg/m² on days 1, 3, 5, 8, 10, and 12 of a 21-day cycle. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR). Secondary endpoints included disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DoR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS) and safety. From June 2020 to July 2022, 128 patients were enrolled and included in the safety set (SS), and 115 patients were in the efficacy analysis set (EAS). At the data cutoff (July 2023), the median follow-up was 19.58 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 16.82-21.95). The ORR was 36.5% (42/115, 95% CI 27.7-46.0), with a complete response rate of 11.3% (13/115). The median DoR was 6.2 months (95% CI 3.5-14.5), median PFS was 2.7 months (95% CI 1.6-3.7), and median OS was 9.9 months (95% CI 7.8-14.8). Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 99.2% (127/128) of patients, and ≥grade 3 TRAEs in 86.7% (111/128). The most common ≥grade 3 TRAEs were thrombocytopenia (75.8%, 97/128), neutropenia (33.6%, 43/128), and leukopenia (22.7%, 29/128). No treatment-related deaths occurred. Ifupinostat demonstrated promising efficacy and a manageable safety profile as a new therapeutic alternative for patients with r/r DLBCL. Clinical Trial Registry Number: ChiCTR1900028179.

articles.title: Novel targeted therapy and cellular immunotherapy enabling allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for relapsed/refractory acute myeloid leukemia.
articles.abstract: Patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are characterized by a disastrous prognosis. For most patients with R/R AML, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only curative option. It is important to conduct mutational analysis again when the disease relapses to identify any new genetic abnormalities that can be targeted with novel treatments. As part of a conditioning regimen or post-transplant maintenance therapy, new targeted agents support HSCT in patients with R/R AML in various forms, including combination chemotherapy to improve complete remission (CR) prior to HSCT. For R/R AML patients with mutated FMS-related tyrosine kinase 3 ( FLT3 ), sorafenib and quizartinib have shown encouraging therapeutic effects either in combination with chemotherapy for bridging to transplantation or as maintenance therapy after HSCT. Ivosidenib and enasidenib, which are inhibitors that target mutated isocitrate dehydrogenase ( IDH ) 1 and 2, respectively, have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of IDH1/IDH2 -mutated R/R AML. Venetoclax, an inhibitor of B-cell lymphoma-2 ( BCL2 ), is widely used in the salvage treatment of R/R AML and has better therapeutic effects and controllable drug toxicity than traditional chemotherapy. In addition, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell immunotherapy (targeting CD33, CD123, and CLL1) has achieved encouraging clinical response rates in phase I and phase II clinical trials for R/R-AML, and subsequent bridging HSCT has significantly improved patient survival.

articles.title: Interventions to increase participation in lung cancer screening programmes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: We aimed to systematically review and meta-analyse the effectiveness of interventions in increasing informed choice and participation in lung cancer screening based on low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). METHODS: Five electronic databases, Medline (PubMed version), Embase, Cinahl (Ebsco version), Scopus and Cochrane CENTRAL, were searched for randomised controlled trials, nonrandomised controlled trials and before-after studies published from 2000 until 15 March 2023. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to assess the effectiveness of interventions to increase rates of LDCT completion. RESULTS: Out of 3483 studies identified, 14 completed and 21 ongoing studies were included in the review. Shared-decision making (SDM)+navigation (OR 4.34, 95% CI 2.50-7.54) and outreach+navigation (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.70-2.84) resulted in a higher proportion of LDCT performed compared to the control group. Educational/informational interventions (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.89-1.19) as well as SDM alone (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.57-2.32) did not improve LDCT uptake, despite the second improving decisional outcomes in both intervention and control groups. Multicomponent interventions showed significantly higher LDCT uptake (OR 2.64, 95% CI 1.79-3.90), compared to unicomponent interventions (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.14). The vast majority of interventions, including those in ongoing trials, are patient-oriented, while community-based, provider-level and system-level interventions remain rare. CONCLUSIONS: Combining high-intensity patient-oriented interventions, such as patient navigation, active outreach and SDM, appears to be the most promising strategy to increase lung cancer screening uptake (low certainty of evidence). However, implementation studies are needed to evaluate interventions targeting both provider and healthcare systems level.
