articles.title: Precancerous cervical lesions and associated factors among HIV-positive women in Southern and Eastern African countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Women living with HIV (WLHIV) face a sixfold increased risk of cervical cancer compared to HIV-negative women. Most WLHIV residing in the Southern and Eastern African regions have a substantial HIV-related cervical cancer burden. Studies on precancerous cervical lesions (PCCL) and associated factors in WLHIV from these regions have inconsistent and inconclusive findings. Therefore, we aimed to synthesize the pooled prevalence of PCCL and associated factors among WLHIV in Southern and Eastern Africa. METHODS: This study was registered under PROSPERO (CRD420251123583) and conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 standards. Primary studies published from inception to 2025 in Southern and Eastern Africa were included. The methodological quality of studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale. Data extraction and statistical analyses were done in Microsoft Excel and STATA 17, respectively. Pooled prevalence, publication bias, subgroup, and sensitivity analysis were conducted. Associations were expressed as odds ratios (OR), and a p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: 44 studies met the inclusion criteria, with a sample size of 47,009. The pooled prevalence of PCCL was 22.25% (95% CI: 19.57, 24.93). Age at first sexual intercourse (< 18 years) (OR = 2.99, (2.34, 3.82)), multiparity (OR = 4.97, (3.21, 7.69)), having multiple sexual partners (OR = 3.06 (2.45, 3.83)), having a history of sexually transmitted infections (STI) (OR = 3.93 (3.23, 4.78)), smoking (OR = 7.01, (3.39, 14.49)), ever taking oral contraceptive pills (OR = 2.69, (1.85, 3.90)), low CD4 count (OR = 1.79, (1.56, 2.05)), and having not initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) (OR = 2.02, (1.56, 2.62)) were significantly associated with an increased risk of PCCL. CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS: The pooled prevalence of PCCL was high. Additionally, early first sexual intercourse, parity, STIs, multiple sexual partners, smoking, oral contraceptive use, CD4 count, and ART were positively associated with the occurrence of PCCL. Therefore, stakeholders shall implement interventions to avert future incidents of PCCL and address the identified factors.

articles.title: Effectiveness of cardiac resynchronization therapy in cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Advances in cancer treatment have increased the number of survivors, making cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) an important concern. While cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is established for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and conduction disorders, its role in CTRCD remains unclear. We conducted a meta-analysis to assess the benefit of CRT in patients with CTRCD. METHODS: We performed a literature search of studies showing CRT outcomes in the specific group of CTRCD patients. The outcomes of interest were left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and LV volume improvement. A random effects meta-analysis was done to estimate 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: This analysis included four studies (one prospective and three retrospective) comprising 110 patients with CTRCD, the majority (91%, n = 100) being survivors of breast cancer or lymphoma/leukemia. Baseline LVEF ranged from 18.6% ± 7.6% to 28.5% ± 3.8% (mean 24% ± 7%). After a mean follow-up of 9 ± 5 months, LVEF increased by 9.95% (95% CI 7.79-12.11) and end-systolic volume decreased by 39.17 mL (95% CI 24.99-53.35). Three studies included a control group of patients with other forms of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy who underwent CRT implantation, showing no significant difference in LVEF improvement between the two groups. CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis suggests that CRT improves LVEF and LV volumes in selected patients with CTRCD, with a magnitude of reverse remodeling that appears similar to that observed in other etiologies of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. However, the evidence is limited to small observational studies, so conclusions about clinical outcomes remain uncertain. Thus, CRT may be considered in cancer patients who meet standard criteria for CRT implantation, but the decision should be individualized and guided by multidisciplinary assessment, cancer prognosis, and competing clinical risks.

articles.title: Association between cancer cachexia and treatment-related adverse outcomes in patients with gastrointestinal cancers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Cachexia represents a critical nutritional problem, especially among patients with gastrointestinal cancer, and is potentially linked to unfavorable outcomes. Nevertheless, the influence of cancer cachexia on treatment-related adverse events in these patients remains insufficiently incorporated into current understanding. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the association between cancer cachexia and treatment-related adverse outcomes in patients with gastrointestinal cancers. METHODS: Five electronic databases were searched for relevant studies. Cohort studies investigating the association of cachexia with postoperative complications, chemotherapy-related adverse events, radiotherapy-related adverse events, length of hospital stay, and readmission in patients with gastrointestinal cancers were included. RESULTS: Thirty-four studies involving 27,473 participants were included. Cancer cachexia was significantly associated with higher odds of postoperative complications (odds ratio [OR] 1.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.11-1.72) and prolonged length of hospital stay (mean difference = 2.09, 95% CI = 0.91-3.26). No significant association was observed between cancer cachexia and chemotherapy-related adverse events (OR = 1.42, 95% CI = 0.57-3.54). All pooled analyses showed considerable to substantial heterogeneity. No studies evaluating radiotherapy-related adverse events and only one study evaluating readmission met the inclusion criteria; therefore, these outcomes could not be quantitatively synthesized. CONCLUSIONS: Cancer cachexia was associated with an increased risk of postoperative complications and prolonged length of hospital stay in patients with gastrointestinal cancers. However, because of the substantial heterogeneity and the very low certainty of the evidence, these findings should be interpreted with caution and cannot be considered definitive.

articles.title: Neoadjuvant Therapy for Gastric Adenocarcinoma with Signet Ring Cells: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Signet ring cell-containing gastric cancer constitutes an increasingly recognized subtype. Although perioperative chemotherapy is the standard of treatment for locally advanced gastric cancer, its efficacy in signet ring cell-containing gastric adenocarcinomas remains controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the impact of neoadjuvant chemotherapy compared to upfront surgery on overall survival. METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane was conducted up to January 2026. Eligible studies included adult patients with signet ring cell-containing gastric cancer undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery compared to upfront gastrectomy. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to pool hazard ratios for overall survival. RESULTS: Six studies, including seven cohorts and 5.388 patients, were included. The pooled analysis demonstrated no significant difference in overall survival between neoadjuvant chemotherapy and upfront surgery (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.68-1.34, I CONCLUSIONS: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was not associated with a significant improvement in overall survival compared with upfront surgery in signet-ring cell-containing gastric cancer. While perioperative chemotherapy remains the recommended therapeutic approach, further studies employing contemporary chemotherapy regimens are warranted to define its role in this distinct histological subtype.

articles.title: Comparative efficacy of interventions for preventing chemotherapy-induced alopecia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Chemotherapy-induced alopecia (CIA) negatively affects patients' appearance and emotional well-being. This network meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy of different preventive interventions for CIA. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, and EBSCO Open Dissertations from inception to March 2025. Randomized controlled trials evaluating interventions to prevent CIA in cancer patients and reporting hair preservation outcomes (as defined by individual trials, including CTCAE grade < 2, < 30 to < 50% hair loss, or WHO grade 0-2) were included. Scalp hypothermia was divided into three groups based on duration post-chemotherapy: short (0-45 min), traditional (46-90 min), and prolonged (> 90 min). Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB2. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Interventions were ranked with surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), and certainty of evidence was evaluated using CINeMA. RESULTS: Of 6696 articles identified, 12 (n = 736) evaluating nine interventions (three scalp hypothermia durations, scalp compression, four pharmacological agents, and usual care) were included. Network meta-analysis indicated that prolonged-scalp hypothermia significantly improved hair preservation compared with usual care (RR = 24.66; 95%CI = 7.07-86.05; low certainty of evidence) and traditional scalp hypothermia (RR = 2.13; 95%CI = 1.15-3.93; very low certainty of evidence), and pharmacological agents (RRs ranging from 14.06 to 23.83; low certainty). However, prolonged-scalp hypothermia tended to show better hair preservation than short duration, though not statistically significant (RR = 2.06, 95%CI = 0.78-5.39). Based on SUCRA, prolonged-scalp hypothermia (97.0%) had the highest ranking, followed by short scalp hypothermia (78.6%) and traditional scalp hypothermia (76.8%). Most studies were rated as having high risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was graded as low to very low. CONCLUSION: Current low certainty evidence suggests that scalp hypothermia could prevent CIA. Prolonged-scalp hypothermia provides a higher degree of protection, whereas a short duration demonstrates a weaker protective effect. However, this difference was not statistically significant. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251103932) and can be accessed via the following link: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251103932 .

articles.title: Comparative perioperative and oncological outcomes of the da Vinci Xi versus Si robotic surgical systems in rectal cancer surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: The da Vinci Xi replaced the Si with a boom-mounted architecture intended to remove the re-docking and multiquadrant limits on pelvic access. Whether it changes outcomes in rectal cancer surgery is unresolved: existing syntheses pooled rectal with colonic resection. Five databases, Google Scholar and citation graphs were searched to August 2026, without language or design restriction, for comparative studies reporting outcomes separately by platform in rectal cancer resection. Screening, extraction and risk-of-bias assessment were done in duplicate. Random-effects models with a Hartung-Knapp adjustment were used; certainty was rated with GRADE. Eight non-randomised cohorts (843 patients; 380 Xi, 463 Si) were included. Pooling all five cohorts reporting operative time, the mean difference was - 27.7 min (95% confidence interval - 80.4 to + 25.0; I² 95%); restricted to the four reporting means with standard deviations, thus conditional on excluding the largest cohort, it was - 50.6 min (- 69.4 to - 31.7). Docking time was shorter with the Xi in all three reporting cohorts, which defined it differently or not at all. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of platform on anastomotic leak (risk ratio 0.53, 0.24 to 1.14), complications, conversion, reoperation, margin involvement and specimen quality; certainty was very low throughout. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of the da Vinci Xi compared with the Si on perioperative and oncological outcomes in rectal cancer, and functional outcomes have not been compared. Because the platforms were compared across periods, centres and levels of experience, no estimate isolates the platform.PROSPERO registration CRD420261480007, registered 18 August 2026, before data extraction.

articles.title: The prognostic value of physical functioning on survival in patients with nonsmall cell lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physical functioning has emerged as a potentially valuable prognostic indicator in patients with nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of objectively measured components of physical functioning on survival outcomes across treatment modalities. METHODS: Medline, Web of Science and Scopus were searched up to May 2025. Eligible studies included adult patients with NSCLC and assessed at least one objectively measured physical functioning indicator in relation to survival outcomes. Indicators were categorised using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework into "body functions and structures", "activities" and "participation" and studies were stratified into "surgery" and "nonsurgery" groups. Meta-analyses were conducted when data permitted it. RESULTS: 58 studies (19 436 patients) were included. Most assessments were performed before treatment. In the surgical group, only "activities"-based measures were evaluated. A meta-analysis restricted to this group showed that survivors had substantially higher (functional) exercise capacity, measured through cardiopulmonary exercise testing and field tests (standardised mean difference 0.79). In nonsurgical cohorts, prognostic value extended across all ICF domains, with low handgrip strength (hazard ratio (HR) 1.27), low (functional) exercise capacity (HR 2.11) and physical inactivity (HR 2.86) associated with significantly higher mortality. Notably, no studies in surgical cohorts evaluated "body functions" or "participation". Heterogeneity and varying thresholds were noted across studies. CONCLUSIONS: Objectively measured physical functioning is a significant prognostic indicator of survival in NSCLC. Routine assessment could enhance risk stratification and guide personalised care. Future research should address longitudinal changes, standardisation of measures and targeted interventions.

articles.title: The role of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in adults with mature T-cell lymphomas.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Mature T-cell lymphomas (MTCL) are a rare, heterogeneous group of malignancies that arise from post-thymic T-lymphocytes, with a generally poor prognosis. For a long time, the standard therapy for most MTCL subtypes has been polychemotherapies. Hopes to prolong overall survival in MTCL have been associated with transplant procedures such as high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell transplantation (autoSCT) or allogeneic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT). OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of alloSCT in the treatment of MTCL in adults (≥ 18 years old) compared to any other treatment, particularly with respect to its efficacy and safety as first-line therapy, and secondarily, for its efficacy and safety as a salvage option. SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, conference proceedings, and two databases of ongoing trials from January 1990 to October 2025 for prospective and retrospective studies evaluating the role of alloSCT for MTCL. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospectively planned trials assessing the role of alloSCT as first-line or salvage treatment for MTCL. As determined at the protocol stage, we excluded retrospective trials because we identified prospective ones. We excluded trials in which less than 80% of participants had MTCL, unless we could obtain a subgroup analysis for these participants. OUTCOMES: We analyzed overall survival, progression-free survival (PFS), response rate, treatment-related mortality (TRM), quality of life (QoL), grade 3 and 4 adverse events, and incidences of acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD and cGVHD, respectively). RISK OF BIAS: We assessed the risk of bias (RoB) in the included studies using Cochrane's RoB 2 tool for RCTs and the Cochrane Childhood Cancer Group's assessment criteria tool for observational studies. We rated the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach for all previously stated outcomes. SYNTHESIS METHODS: We followed standard Cochrane methodology, and two independent review authors performed all steps regarding study selection and risk of bias assessment in duplicate. INCLUDED STUDIES: We included one RCT of alloSCT as first-line treatment for MTCL (103 participants), and two prospectively planned trials of alloSCT as salvage treatment (119 participants): one Mendelian-randomized controlled trial for cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) (102 participants) and one prospective observational trial for non-cutaneous MTCL (17 participants). We identified three ongoing trials. All of them are non-randomized, phase-II studies. They will mostly include relapsed or refractory lymphomas. Two other studies are awaiting classification. Overall, we rated both included RCTs to have some concerns of bias due to bias arising from the randomization process, and missing outcome data. The RoB for the prospective observational study was rated serious due to the study design, small number of participants, and reporting and detection bias. SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: As we did not identify enough RCTs, we did not conduct a meta-analysis. We rated the evidence for all outcomes to be of low to very low certainty, due to the very small number of events and limitations in study design. AlloSCT compared to autoSCT for adults with MTCL (first-line) We included one RCT with 103 participants. AlloSCT compared to autoSCT may result in little to no difference in two-year overall survival (hazard ratio (HR) 1.3 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.7 to 2.4; low-certainty evidence) or PFS HR 0.9 (95% CI 0.5 to 1.5; low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT compared to autoSCT may result in a large increase in TRM (RR 18.70, 95% CI 1.11 to 315.72; low-certainty evidence), but may have no effect on overall response rate (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.45; low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT compared to autoSCT may result in little to no difference in the number of adverse events (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.75). 84% of all participants receiving alloSCT had aGVHD and 47% had cGVHD (very low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT for adults with non-cutaneous MTCL (relapsed or refractory setting) We included one phase-II study with 17 participants. Overall survival and PFS at two years were presented graphically in the included study, and were approximately 80% and 64%, respectively (very low-certainty evidence for both). The overall response rate was 76% after one month (70% in complete remission and 6% in partial remission; very low-certainty evidence). The two-year TRM rate was presented graphically in the included study, without making reference to absolute numbers, and was approximately 6% (very low-certainty evidence). 35% of all participants had aGVHD and 41% had cGVHD (very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were not reported. AlloSCT compared to other treatment for adults with CTCL (relapsed or refractory setting) We included one RCT with 102 participants. AlloSCT compared to any other treatment may make little or no difference to overall survival (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.29; very low-certainty evidence), but may increase PFS (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.69; very low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT may make little or no difference to the number of adverse events (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.50; very low-certainty evidence). The one-year cumulative incidence of cGVHD was 31.4% (very low-certainty evidence). The overall response rate and TRM were not reported. AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: In this systematic review, we identified one RCT of alloSCT as first-line treatment for MTCL, and one Mendelian RCT and one prospectively planned phase-II trial of alloSCT for relapsed or refractory MTCL. We encountered difficulties while extracting data from these studies, because there were major differences in study designs, intervention and control groups. We identified low- to very low-certainty evidence on the effectiveness and safety of alloSCT for adults with MTCL. We had some concerns about the risk of bias in the two RCTs and serious concerns about bias in the phase-II study. As there are three ongoing studies evaluating alloSCT, mostly for relapsed or refractory MTCL, it is possible that an update of this review will be published in the near future. However, none of the ongoing studies are of an RCT design.
